chapter_theme: Seven songs at Tiruvarur (திருவாரூர்): three in long syllables with a shared refrain (one on a wasted life, one in a lovesick girl's voice, one on a lullaby's endearments), a short plea for the feet of knowledge, two courtesan songs, one of which tells the story of Manu's justice, and a song that turns the questions of desire into questions about the inner light.
structure_note: 816 to 818 share the closing line சேயே வேளே பூவே கோவே தேவே தேவப் பெருமாளே and are made of long syllables; 819 is four lines; 820 and 821 confess infatuation; 822 recasts the lover's questions as questions about the light within.

816.reading: The poet asks whether it is right that his days go in vain, a dog's life, without his singing the vel, putting the koothalam garland Murugan loves on his shoulders, speaking his name and falling at the feet beyond the Veda, the mind turning nowhere else. The praise calls Murugan friend, lord of the gods, the kadamba-wearer who went to the millet field for the deer-like Valli, lord of the land of kalpaka trees, lord of the lowly, the great life of glorious Arur, child, Vel, flower, king and god of gods.
816.nuance: The song is made almost entirely of long syllables in two-syllable words ending in -ஆதே (கூசாதே, பாடாதே, பேசாதே, வீழாதே), a list of what the poet has failed to do. The first line (கூசாதே பார் ஏசாதே மால் கூறா நூல் கற்று) is hard to divide; it may describe learning, unashamed, books that tell no delusion.

817.reading: In the voice of a girl in love, the singer calls to the sharp-beaked crane: the one who left has not come back, her life has withered to a husk, her mother has turned against her, the town's slander is heard, and the young north wind cuts like a saw and burns like fire; she asks whether she must be ruined like those who sing the names of misers and never prosper. The praise names the unbeaten vel that let no Sura live and gave grace to the gods, the light of Arur with Uma in his half, and Murugan as son of Siva who burned the enemies' towns.
817.nuance: This is akam poetry: the crane as messenger (கூர்வாய் நாராய்), the mother's anger and the north wind (இளவாடை) are classical, and the poet's own confession is absent. ஈயா வாழ்வோர் பேரே பாடா ஈடேறாரின் கெடலாமோ: the girl compares her fate to poets who sing for misers, the poet's own recurring complaint (827, 828). Word division in the long syllables is uncertain.

818.reading: The first half strings the endearments of a lullaby, 'are you milk, honey, syrup, the nectar of the gods' sea, the glory of the world, the sun, the pearl of the sky', and asks whether it is fit to be reproached without having sung that lullaby, talo talelo, with a mother's love. The praise shows Murugan, hearing Valli's bird-scaring cry, going in love to the millet field and falling at her feet, and names him the great life of Arur with its fish-filled tanks.
818.nuance: பாலோ தேனோ பாகோ ... தாலோ தாலேலோ: the opening is a lullaby's string of questions, the form of pillaitamil, and 822 opens with the same words for a woman's speech. Who is reproached and what is asked in lines 5 to 8 is unclear; the line with பே¡£யாதே is damaged. ஆயாள் தாள்மேல் வீழா: Murugan falling at Valli's feet is a recurring image of his humility in love.

819.reading: In four lines the poet asks Murugan to be gracious for long ages in every way and to give him, as a great gift and treasure, the feet of great knowledge. The praise names him Brahma's kin, the hero of true virtue, the light in the adharas, lord at Arur.
819.nuance: மாஞானக் கழல்: the feet are named as knowledge itself. ஆதாரத்து ஒளியானே: the Lord as the light in the yogic centres. வேதா மைத்துன: Brahma, as Vishnu's son, is Murugan's cousin in the poet's scheme.

820.reading: The poet describes women whose long eyes, like arrows, are nets that end men's lifetimes, and whose speech, musk and sandal on their breasts draw his mind, and asks whether that mind will not think of Murugan's anklet-bearing lotus feet. The praise names the Nirutas' host dead and the hills crushed, Rama who made the lord of rivers cry out with a single arrow as Narayana, Murugan's uncle, and Arur, where in every grove of the Siva shrine the bees hum in order.
820.nuance: மனிதர் வாணாள் அடங்க வருவார்: the women are said to come to end men's lives, the courtesan as a form of Death. நதிபதி கதற ஒரு கணை: Rama threatening the ocean with one arrow before the bridge.

821.reading: The poet, who wanders infatuated with women whose hands are lotuses, faces moons and breasts hills, asks whether a day will come when, with night and day, enmity, impurity and infatuation gone, tears flowing and heart melted, he gains the sweetness of the word 'the young one who sank into the breasts of the hunter girl, too beautiful to draw on the madal' and reaches the two feet. The praise tells how a cow, whose calf had been killed, rang the bell of Manu's justice; the king heard of the wrong, melted crying 'Hara Siva', and ordered the chariot driven over his own guilty son, splitting his body, while the cow wept; Murugan is the six-faced son of Siva, Ganapati's younger brother, lord at that Arur of grace, whose vel made the sea cry out.
821.nuance: குறமகள் ... மடலூடே எழுத அரியவள்: Valli is the girl too lovely to draw on the madal, the banner of the lover's palmyra horse, so the love theme is carried into the praise. The praise tells, unusually at length, the Tiruvarur story of the Chola king of Manu's justice, who executed his own son for a calf; the king is not named beyond மனுவின் நெறி.

822.reading: The poet, delighting in a woman and asking whether her speech is milk, honey, jackfruit, the gods' nectar, cane syrup or the milk of knowledge given to the child who melted, whether her eyes are vel or arrow and her face sun or moon, asks for grace to melt instead asking: what is the light of the six faces, is the light growing within me I or you, is the place that shines like crystal a land or release, tell me the middle word, Lord of the golden hall. The praise has the gods rain flowers, sages hail 'Hara Siva', the demons and the roaring sea cry out and the hill split, and names Murugan the son born to the maiden who is Uma, Lakshmi and Saraswati, at Arur, where the pure say 'this is the bliss of Siva's state, let us stay here'.
822.nuance: The song uses one form for two loves: the lover's questions (மொழி பாலோ தேனோ, விழி வேலோ கோலோ) are matched by the seeker's (நானோ நீயோ, நாடோ வீடோ). ஊனோடு உருகிய மகன் உண அருள் ஞானப் பால் refers to the milk of knowledge given to the child Sambandar. எனது அகம் வளர் ஒளி நானோ நீயோ: whether the inner light is self or Lord is put as a question, not answered.

links.note: The Kural defines justice as investigating and showing favour to no one; the praise in 821 tells of the Chola king who heard the cow's bell and drove the chariot over his own son, the extreme case of 'no one' including one's own child.

Both open with பாலோ தேனோ, the string of sweet questions: in 818 they are a lullaby's endearments for a child, in 822 a lover's praise of a woman's speech, which the song then turns into questions about the inner light.
